text.p: Bench scale tests on production of aluminum for half the present cost were making progress with commercial production due on stream by 1998, John Rendall, chairman of chief executive of Solv-Ex Corp said.

Last week the company began opening a mine on its Athabasca oil sands lease in Alberta, Canada, with commercial production of bitumen due in the first quarter of 1997, along with potassium filler and alumina mid-year.

Later in 1997, oil for pipeline shipment at the rate of 14,000 barrels per day will be produced from bitumen. "We have established $3 per barrel for mining costs," Rendall said. "Initially we will be getting over $10 per barrel for the bitumen for all our output."
Rendall said Gibson Petroleum has agreed to buy the bitumen and oil.

Solv-Ex will consume its metallurgical grade alumina to make aluminum metal, using its own technology. "We don't intend to sell the alumina to the market at any time - it's for making aluminum metal," Rendall told Reuters.
However, "several thousand tonnes per month" of catalyst grade alumina will be marketed, Rendall said.
Once the bench scale 10 AMP aluminum production cell is operating continuously by the end of September, Solv-Ex will move ahead on a prototype for a commercial cell, due on stream next year.
A 25,000 tonnes per year potline - a string of cells - will be operational in 1998, Rendall said.

The metal will be made for at least half the usual cost because of the cheaply sourced alumina, a lower temperature in the cell, non-consumable cell anodes, and electricity from co-generation costing just one cent per kilowatt hour.
Solv-Ex's equity dealings and technological claims have prompted controversy and skepticism in the aluminum industry.

On August 12 Solv-Ex filed lawsuits against what it described as short-sellers of its shares. The share price reached a peak of $38 in January and then plunged to a low of 6 1/4. On Monday the shares were trading at 11 1/8, up 3/4 on the day.

Rendall said over $100 million has been raised for the project - short of the $200 million target set for June this year. Negative publicity caused delays in generating adequate financing for the project, Rendall admitted in a letter to shareholders on Monday.
"The capital raised is sufficient to get cash flow," Rendall told Reuters.
So far the Athabasca mine site has been cleared, a maintenance building set up, 200 people employed, $26 million spent on construction equipment, and $5 million spent on mining equipment.
